console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.

Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations

Event Loop

Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services

    console.log(data);

   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style

console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services

"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)

Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.

Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style

   console.log(data);

Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking

Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes

Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services

HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations

Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);

Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Done

“Has any async task completed?”

Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.

Event Loop

Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.

Handles many users concurrently

Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations

Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations

How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.

How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.

console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.

Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations

Event Loop

Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services

    console.log(data);

   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style

console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services

"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)

Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.

Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style

   console.log(data);

Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking

Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes

Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services

HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations

Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
Simple Example
Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);

Synchronous (Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

const data = fs.readFileSync('file.txt', 'utf8');
console.log(data);

console.log('Done');
Node.js waits until the file is fully read.
"Done" prints only after reading finishes.
Asynchronous (Non-Blocking)
const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
    console.log(data);
});

console.log('Done');

Output:

Done
[file content]
File reading happens in the background.
Node.js continues executing other code immediately.
Why Async I/O Matters
Handles many users concurrently
Better performance for I/O-heavy applications
Uses fewer system resources
Prevents server slowdown during waiting operations
Common Async Operations in Node.js
File system operations
Database queries
HTTP requests
API calls
Timers (setTimeout)
Streams
How Node.js Achieves This

Node.js uses:

Event Loop
Callbacks
Promises
Async/Await
libuv thread pool internally

The event loop keeps checking:

“Has any async task completed?”
If yes → execute its callback.
Async Styles in Node.js
1. Callback Style
fs.readFile('a.txt', (err, data) => {
   console.log(data);
});
2. Promise Style
readFile('a.txt')
   .then(data => console.log(data));
3. Async/Await Style
const data = await readFile('a.txt');
console.log(data);
Key Difference
Synchronous I/O	Asynchronous I/O
Blocking	Non-blocking
Waits for task completion	Continues execution
Slower under heavy load	Scales better
Easier flow	Better performance
Real-World Analogy
Synchronous: You order coffee and wait at the counter until it’s ready.
Asynchronous: You order coffee, get a token, and do other work until your coffee is ready.
Async I/O (Asynchronous Input/Output) in Node.js means Node.js can start a task like reading a file, querying a database, or calling an API without waiting for it to finish before moving to the next task.
Instead of blocking execution, Node.js:
Starts the I/O operation
Continues running other code
Gets notified when the operation completes
This makes Node.js highly efficient for:
Web servers
APIs
Real-time apps
Chat applications
Streaming services
